q: A capacitor stores electrical energy in the form of a magnetic field.
e: False. The right claim is this: A capacitor stores electrical energy in the form of an electric field. Two conductors and a dielectric hold opposite charge, so energy sits in the electric field. The printed line wrongly says a capacitor stores electrical energy in the form of a magnetic field.

q: When the capacitor is charged, the charging process can be viewed as the apparent transfer of charge between two conductors.
e: True. Two conductors and a dielectric hold opposite charge, so energy sits in the electric field. Can be viewed as the apparent transfer of charge between two conductors.

q: During charging, the charge is transferred from a conductor at higher potential to a conductor at lower potential.
e: False. The right claim is this: The charge has been transferred from a conductor at lower potential to a conductor at higher potential. Charge is conserved; it is what a current carries and what a capacitor stores on its plates. The printed line wrongly says during charging, the charge is transferred from a conductor at higher potential to a conductor at lower potential.

q: Work has been done for the transfer of charge between the two conductors of a capacitor.
e: True. The plates must conduct so charge can spread; the gap must insulate or the field collapses. For the transfer of charge between the two conductors of a capacitor.

q: The magnitude of the charge on the two conductors increases gradually and the potential difference between them also increases gradually during charging.
e: True. While charging, plate voltage climbs toward the battery value as 1 minus a decaying exponential. Gradually and the potential difference between them also increases gradually during charging.

q: The work done in charging the capacitor is given by the shaded area under the Q-V curve.
e: True. Two conductors and a dielectric hold opposite charge, so energy sits in the electric field. The capacitor is given by the shaded area under the Q-V curve.

q: The work done in charging the capacitor is equal to $QV$.
e: False. The right claim is this: The work done in charging the capacitor is given by the shaded area under the curve. While charging, plate voltage climbs toward the battery value as 1 minus a decaying exponential. The printed line wrongly says the work done in charging the capacitor is equal to QV.

q: The energy stored by the capacitor is equal to $\frac{1}{2}QV$.
e: True. Two conductors and a dielectric hold opposite charge, so energy sits in the electric field. The energy stored by the capacitor is equal to (1)/(2)QV.

q: Before a capacitor is charged, the potential difference between two conductors is maximum.
e: False. The right claim is this: Before a capacitor is charged, the potential difference between its two conductors is zero. Potential difference is the electrical push between two points; no push, no current. The printed line wrongly says before a capacitor is charged, the potential difference between two conductors is maximum.

q: The average potential difference of the capacitor before and after it is charged is $\frac{0 + V}{2}$.
e: True. Potential difference is the electrical push between two points; no push, no current. The capacitor before and after it is charged is (0 + V)/(2).

q: The work done W for transferring charge of Q between the two conductors is $W = V_{avg} Q$.
e: True. Charge is conserved; it is what a current carries and what a capacitor stores on its plates. The relation in this line is W = Vavg Q.

q: The electrical energy stored by the capacitor is in the form of an electric field.
e: True. Electrical energy is what a current carries through a circuit, later turned into heat, light or motion. Stored by the capacitor is in the form of an electric field.

q: Since $C = \frac{Q}{V}$, the energy W of the capacitor can be expressed as $W = \frac{1}{2}CV^2$.
e: True. Two conductors and a dielectric hold opposite charge, so energy sits in the electric field. The relation in this line is C = (Q)/(V), the energy W of the capacitor c.

q: The energy of a capacitor can also be expressed as $W = \frac{1}{2}QC$.
e: False. The right claim is this: The energy W of the capacitor can also be expressed in terms of Q and C as W = (1)/(2)Q^2/C. Two conductors and a dielectric hold opposite charge, so energy sits in the electric field. The printed line wrongly says the energy of a capacitor can also be expressed as W = (1)/(2)QC.

q: Placing a resistor in the charging circuit speeds up the charging process.
e: False. The right claim is this: Placing a resistor in the charging circuit slows down the charging process. While charging, plate voltage climbs toward the battery value as 1 minus a decaying exponential. The printed line wrongly says placing a resistor in the charging circuit speeds up the charging process.

q: The greater the values of resistance and capacitance, the longer it takes to charge the capacitor.
e: True. Charge is conserved; it is what a current carries and what a capacitor stores on its plates. Of resistance and capacitance, the longer it takes to charge the capacitor.

q: The product of the resistance R and the capacitance C is called the time constant $\tau$ of a capacitor.
e: True. RC is the charging and discharging time scale; after a few RC the exponential has almost settled. The capacitance C is called the time constant tau of a capacitor.

q: The time constant of a capacitor charging or discharging process is measured in farads.
e: False. The right claim is this: The product of the resistance R and the capacitance C is called the time constant τ of a capacitor charging or discharging process. It is measured in second. RC is the charging and discharging time scale; after a few RC the exponential has almost settled.

q: During charging, the voltage rises with time according to the equation $V_c = V_0(1 - e^{-t/RC})$.
e: True. Voltage is potential difference, energy per unit charge between two points. The relation in this line is Vc = V0(1 - e^-t/RC).

q: In the charging equation, $V_0$ is the voltage provided by the capacitor.
e: False. The right claim is this: The voltage of the capacitor falls off with time according to the equation Vc = V0 e^-t/RC. Voltage is potential difference, energy per unit charge between two points. The printed line wrongly says in the charging equation, V0 is the voltage provided by the capacitor.

q: After being charged, the capacitor can be discharged through the load resistor R.
e: True. While discharging, voltage decays toward zero as a pure exponential with the same RC. After being charged, the capacitor can be discharged through the load resistor R.

q: During the discharging process, the voltage of the capacitor falls off with time according to the equation $V_c = V_0(e^{t/RC})$.
e: False. The right claim is this: The voltage of the capacitor falls off with time during discharging according to the equation Vc = V0(1 - e^-t/RC). While discharging, voltage decays toward zero as a pure exponential with the same RC. The printed line wrongly says during the discharging process, the voltage of the capacitor falls off with time according to the equation Vc = V0(e^t/RC).

q: The voltage characteristics of charging and discharging a capacitor are linear with respect to time.
e: False. The right claim is this: The product of the resistance R and the capacitance C is called the time constant of a capacitor charging or discharging process. While charging, plate voltage climbs toward the battery value as 1 minus a decaying exponential. The printed line wrongly says the voltage characteristics of charging and discharging a capacitor are linear with respect to time.

q: Energy stored in a capacitor can be analyzed from the Q-V graph.
e: True. Two conductors and a dielectric hold opposite charge, so energy sits in the electric field. Energy stored in a capacitor can be analyzed from the Q-V graph.

q: The energy stored in a capacitor is equal to the total area of the rectangle in the Q-V graph.
e: False. The right claim is this: The energy stored by the capacitor is equal to (1)/(2)QV. Two conductors and a dielectric hold opposite charge, so energy sits in the electric field. The printed line wrongly says the energy stored in a capacitor is equal to the total area of the rectangle in the Q-V graph.
